slay-bench

Measuring the Planning Horizon
at Which LLMs Collapse

A single-domain, multi-horizon planning benchmark built on Slay the Spire — with a ground-truth oracle at every horizon.

Shoyam Mishra  ·  BITS Pilani
16 July 2026  ·  targeting NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks
Motivation

Every planning benchmark tests one horizon

  • LLMs can plan a little — but "planning ability" is not one thing.
  • PlanBench · short symbolic rearrangement.   NATURAL PLAN, TravelPlanner · single-episode scheduling.
  • Each reports one score at one decision horizon.
  • So when a model fails, you cannot tell how far ahead it stayed coherent before it broke.

At what planning horizon does an LLM stop planning?

Reframes "can LLMs plan?" (yes / no) into "at what horizon does planning break?" — a graded, per-horizon question one benchmark score cannot answer.

Why this game

One game, four nested planning horizons

  • turn → combat → deck synergy → full run, all in one shared simulator.
  • Deterministic — seeded RNG; same seed → same game, same enemies, same draws.
  • A ground-truth optimum is computable at every horizon — this is the enabling property.

Not a toy — an established testbed

  • Anthropic (2026) used STS as a long-horizon planning testbed for a flagship launch → domain validation.
  • Academic use: Bateni & Whitehead (FDG 2024); Orak (2025).

Anthropic's scaffolded (memory + vision) agent measures the ceiling of an engineered agent; our unscaffolded, no-memory harness measures the floor of raw per-horizon planning — the deliberate complement. Their "~3× to the final act with memory" corroborates our run-level floor effect. Prior work is detailed next.

The core contribution

The unoccupied cell: multi-horizon decomposition with a per-horizon oracle

What every other game benchmark does

  • One aggregate score per whole game — Orak, GameBench, FDG-STS.
  • One game per skill — DSGBench, SmartPlay: horizon is confounded with domain.
  • A single decision horizon — PlanBench, NATURAL PLAN.

What slay-bench does

  • One shared simulator, four nested horizons, each with its own ground-truth oracle.
  • A score gap between horizons isolates a planning-horizon effect, not domain shift.
  • + optimality-relative scoring & a seed-matched format ablation.

Claim 1 (lead): the decomposition + per-horizon oracle is unoccupied in the literature. Claim 2 (a feature, not a first): optimality-relative scoring — kin to GraphArena, CO-Bench, LLM-Chess. Claim 3 (extension): the format ablation confirms & extends Bateni & Whitehead.

Positioning: we confirm, extend, and quantify Bateni & Whitehead — they improved play by removing name priors; we show models label decks by name priors while playing them correctly. Never framed as a discovery.

Not novel (stated upfront): STS as an LLM testbed; the name-vs-logic effect (FDG 2024, first); LLMs being weak at long-horizon strategy. Novel: the bottom row — and the format ablation is a format extension of their content ablation, on identical seeds.

Benchmark design

The four dimensions — each with its own oracle

DimensionWhat it testsGround-truth oracleMetric
Turn-levelBest card sequence, one turnExhaustive DFS, ≤720 perms, 20k-node budgetdamage_ratio 0–1
CombatWin a full fight, turn by turnGreedy-bot baselinewin_rate, hp_ratio
SynergyArchetype ID / best pick / worst removal40 hand-crafted decks (20/char, 5/archetype)archetype / pick / removal acc
Run-levelSurvive Act 1 (15 floors)Absolute survival + progresssurvival, progress

Horizons are nested: a turn sits inside a combat, a combat inside a run; synergy is the deck-level judgment that spans them. Each oracle is independent — turn is provably optimal, synergy is expert-labeled.

Caveat: the turn oracle scores damage only; defensive play is out of scope and stated in the prompt, so models are not penalized for unscored blocking.

The apparatus

A faithful, audited simulator — built, not wrapped

  • Custom Python engine — Ironclad + Silent, Acts 1–3, ~170 cards with exact effects.
  • Java-compatible LCG seeded RNG, 9 independent streams (draw / HP / reward / …) → full determinism.
  • Event-bus (pub/sub) relic & power interaction engine.
  • 138 regression tests, all passing.

Both prompt formats — structured JSON vs. raw English — receive identical RNG seeds. Only the state rendering changes → a clean format ablation.

A custom sim (not a game wrapper) is what makes a per-horizon oracle and frozen RNG possible. Fidelity is enforced by the audits, not assumed.

Design · ◦ optional

One seeded state, two renderings

structured JSON

{ "enemy": {"name":"Cultist","hp":48, "block":0,"intent":"attack 6"}, "player": {"hp":72,"block":0,"energy":3}, "hand": [ {"i":0,"card":"Strike","cost":1,"dmg":6}, {"i":1,"card":"Bash","cost":2,"dmg":8, "applies":"Vulnerable 2"}, {"i":2,"card":"Defend","cost":1,"block":5} ] }

raw English

You face a Cultist with 48 HP and no block. It intends to attack for 6. You have 72 HP, no block, and 3 energy. Your hand: 0. Strike — costs 1, deals 6 damage. 1. Bash — costs 2, deals 8 damage and applies Vulnerable 2. 2. Defend — costs 1, gains 5 block. Which cards do you play, in order?

Illustrative excerpt of the two prompt_builder renderings. Both are serialized from the same seeded GameState — identical facts, only the format differs. Any score gap between formats is a representation effect.

Experimental setup

5 families · 2 characters · 2 formats · n=20 · 5 seeds

Models

  • qwen2.5-7b · llama-3.1-8b · mistral-7b (instruct)
  • qwen3-32b (reasoning)
  • deepseek-r1-distill 14B & 7B (reasoning distills)

Protocol

  • n = 20 / dimension × 5 seeds (42/1042/2042/3042/4042) → mean ± std.
  • Self-hosted, vLLM on the university Slurm cluster (NVIDIA A100 80 GB).
  • parse_ok = 1.0 for all instruct models — instrument clean.

Seeds spaced ≥1000 (a multiple of 20) so per-sample ranges don't overlap → real std, not a fake std≈0. 24 on-disk multi-seed aggregates (4 combos × 6 configs).

Results · the central figure

Models hold at short horizons and collapse as the horizon lengthens

Normalization (common 0–1 vs-baseline axis): turn = damage_ratio as-is · combat = win × min(1, hp_ratio) · synergy = accuracy (chance = floor) · run = clamp₀₁((progress − greedy_floorchar) / (1 − greedy_floorchar)). Greedy anchors measured per character: IC .780, Si .704.

Normalized planning score vs. horizon (structured format). y = 0 is the non-planning floor (greedy / chance), 1 = optimal. Combat normalized as win × min(1, hp) → greedy ≈ 1.0. Lines converge toward the shared collapse floor at run.
Results · Finding 1

Reasoning ≠ a free win

Combat win rate · structured · the distills are the only models below 1.0.
.823
DeepSeek-14B — best turn dmg (IC); .839 on Silent
9.75
its IC run floors — below greedy 12.48
  • Best at the short horizon, worst at the long one — worst cell Silent-raw win .34, hp .21.
  • Mechanism (parse probe): 100% of true JSON failures are truncations mid-<think> → budget-bound deliberation is the cause of the collapse.

Probe caveat: single seed, diagnostic cells (turn n=20 / combat n=3), never folded into the matrix tables; matrix combat counter cited as "invalid-action errors."

Results · Finding 2

Where the models separate — at the deck-building horizon

Synergy accuracy, Silent, structured. Qwen3-32B (crimson) posts the matrix maxima — archetype .80, removal .55 — the one line that bends away from the 7–8B pack. Reference lines: exact chance .25 (4-way archetype) / .33 (3-way pick); removal is free-text card-naming, so its line is a random-distinct-card baseline (1-of-7 = .14), not an exact floor. Variance concentrates at the reasoning horizons (turn .18–.84, archetype .25–.80) and is ≈0 at combat & run.
Results · Finding 3

Models play strategies they cannot name

Per-archetype archetype-ID accuracy · recomputed from 2,400 per-sample synergy records. Gold bars fall below the 4-way chance floor.

  • Payoff-mechanic archetypes Exhaust .017 & Discard .14 are below chance = systematic mislabeling.
  • Yet card-pick on those same decks is .43 vs .33 chance — models play what they cannot name.
  • deepseek-7b collapses on execution (combat win .14–.28) yet removal .41–.54 = 2nd in the matrix.

Independently confirms Bateni & Whitehead (FDG 2024): name priors dominate — they improved play by randomizing names; we quantify the dissociation with a per-horizon oracle.

Results · format ablation

Format sensitivity is a property of the model, not the prompt

Seed-matched ablation — same RNG, only the state rendering changes. Labeled value = the two-character mean (structured−raw); markers show each character (● Ironclad, ◆ Silent). 5 of 6 models favor structured on removal; DeepSeek-R1-14B is the sole reversal (−.19 mean; IC −.13, Silent −.26 — verbose <think> favors prose). Sign is model- and character-dependent elsewhere (Llama/Mistral prefer raw at turn).
Results · run-level

Run-level is the shared collapse floor — on par, never beating

Avg floors reached vs. the measured greedy anchors (dashed): Ironclad 12.48, Silent 11.26. Instruct models sit on par (lifts ≤ .13); only DeepSeek-R1-14B (crimson) falls below — over-deliberation into death. Greedy floor measured with a deterministic bot on the exact run-seeds, 0 API cost.
Rigor

The instrument was audited before the models were judged

5
full adversarial audits
100+
engine / instrument bugs fixed before paper runs
138
regression tests, all passing
  • Burning-Blood artifact — a post-measurement heal made any Ironclad win look like it "beat the bot" by +9.5%. Killed.
  • EventBus stacking — listeners accumulated across a run → fake 100% survival at full HP.
  • Synergy positional confound — always-answer-"0" scored 75–100%; offers now rotated.

"The instrument lies before the subject does" — any boundary value (1.0, 0.0, std≈0, beats-its-own-oracle) is a harness bug until a per-sample audit clears it.

We even audited our own oracle: the turn oracle undercounted Silent's optimum at a 6-card cap → rewritten as the pruned 20k-node DFS. We audit the oracle before trusting the score.

Honest limitations

What this study does not yet show

  • Run-level does not discriminate — every small model floors at ≈ greedy (measured: IC 12.48 floors / .780; Silent 11.26 / .704). Reframed as the shared collapse floor — on par, never beating (lifts ≤ .13).
  • Qwen3-32b is synergy-only — its curve is one point, at the horizon where separation lives.
  • deepseek-7b synergy accs are conditioned on its parseable ~14–18 / 20 fixtures (parse_ok .69–.92).
  • Small open models only (≤32B) — frontier separation is the decisive open question.

"One game?" — the contribution is a reusable method; already instantiated on 2 characters (the blind-spot finding replicates across both). Monster Train / Into the Breach are the flagged next instantiations.

Contributions

A reusable method, not one game

  • Single-domain multi-horizon decomposition with a per-horizon ground-truth oracle.
  • Optimality-relative scoring (how far from optimal, not win/loss).
  • Seed-matched format ablation (a format extension of FDG's content ablation).
  • Open-source simulator + harness + oracles + 138 tests.

The recipe: any game with nested decision horizons can be decomposed into per-horizon dimensions on a shared simulator. STS is the first instantiation.

Adding Silent required zero new harness code — the existence proof that the method transfers. Monster Train / Into the Breach are the next candidates.

Next steps

One decisive experiment left — and it wins either way

M3b — frontier runs (Claude / GPT)

  • Separation confirms the horizon-capability claim (frontier holds one horizon longer).
  • Frontier also floors → the collapse is universal — itself the headline.
  • No losing outcome — the curve was built to show exactly this.

Ready to go

  • Registered token-budget protocol (no repeat of the DeepSeek truncation trap).
  • Conditional Acts 1–3 probe, gated on the M3b outcome.
  • Workshop-ready now; NeurIPS D&B trajectory once frontier lands.

github.com/shoyammishra/slay-the-spire-bench  ·  extends (does not discover) prior STS work (Bateni & Whitehead 2024).

In closing
slay-bench measures not whether a model plans — but how far ahead it can, before it collapses.

Appendix · A5

Parse-probe detail — budget-bound deliberation

1.0
truncation fraction in all four probe cells
10 v 7
7b structured vs raw turn truncations — structured worse
  • Every true JSON failure = a token-budget truncation mid-<think>; zero malformed-but-complete outputs.
  • Combat truncation_errors == json_parse_errors exactly in every cell.
  • The matrix combat counter is cited as "invalid-action errors" (it conflates truncations with valid-JSON-but-illegal actions; probe decomposes it ≈70–75% truncation / 25–30% illegal).

Cells: deepseek-7b Ironclad + deepseek-14b Silent, both formats. Caveats: single seed (42), combat n=3, diagnostic cells never in the matrix tables.

Appendix · A6

Audit trail & normalization detail

Five adversarial audits (2026-06-10 → 12)

  • Each = a full source re-read; 100+ bugs fixed before any paper-grade run.
  • Cheapest-first: mock → smoke → cheap dims → run-level.
  • Comparability preserved: no prompt bytes changed since the matrix; instrumentation additive.
  • Per-item specs in bug_audit_* docs; 138 regression tests.

turndamage_ratio (as-is)
combatwin × min(1, hp_ratio)
synergyaccuracy (chance = floor)
runclamp₀₁((prog − gchar)/(1 − gchar))

Measured greedy anchors g: IC .780 (12.48 floors) · Si .704 (11.26 floors) — deterministic bot on the exact run-seeds, 0 API cost. Combat centers the bot at ≈1.0 by design.

Appendix · A7

"One game?" — two answers

Precedent

  • Single-game benchmark papers publish — LLM-Chess vs Stockfish, LLMs on Sudoku / Wordle.
  • Narrowness alone is not a rejection if the finding is sharp.

The stronger answer — the method

  • Any game with nested decision timescales fits the recipe.
  • Silent added with zero new harness code → the recipe transfers.
  • Next: Monster Train (adds a spatial horizon), Into the Breach (provable turn optimum).

Turns the reviewer's "too narrow" into "demonstrated within STS (2 characters), future work across games."
